# Freedom of the press (`free_press`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by printing_press, woodblock_printing, freedom_of_speech_thought, rule_of_law, habeas_corpus_fair_trial
- Core idea: Anyone may print without asking a censor first; a writer answers only afterwards, before an ordinary court and jury, under a known law of libel in which truth is a defence. A government that cannot silence critics hears about its errors, corrupt officials and coming famines early and cheaply; and since no censor is infallible, suppressing what he thinks false also suppresses truths (Milton). The practical minimum is the end of licensing before publication. Public access to official records, as in Sweden's 1766 law, makes the freedom useful.
- Pitfalls:
  - Proposing it under a Renaissance prince or to the Church: unlicensed printing is sedition or heresy, and the proposer is the first test case
  - Believing truth wins by itself: early presses also poured out libels, forgeries, astrology and witch-hunting manuals
  - Thinking the end of censorship is enough: stamp taxes, seditious-libel trials and control of paper or the post silence a press as well
  - Confusing it with a right to defame private persons; every system that kept a free press also kept a libel law
- History: china: 213 BC – Qin burning of books, the counter-example; from the Song, printing is mostly a private trade punished after the fact, with bans on calendars and state papers and literary inquisitions under the Qing; islamic: 1727 – the Ottoman sultan permits Müteferrika's press for non-religious books only; 1860s first private newspapers in Istanbul and Cairo, under press laws; india: 1780 – Hicky's Bengal Gazette, suppressed 1782; 1835 Metcalfe ends licensing of the press; europe: 1559 – papal Index of Prohibited Books; 1644 Milton's Areopagitica; 1695 England lets the Licensing Act lapse; 1766 Sweden's Freedom of the Press Act, the first such law, with public access to documents; 1770 Denmark-Norway abolishes censorship (restricted again from 1771); 1789 French Declaration, art. 11; americas: 1735 – a New York jury acquits the printer Zenger; 1791 First Amendment
- Read:
  - John Milton, Areopagitica (1644)
  - Fredrick S. Siebert, Freedom of the Press in England, 1476–1776 (1952)
